newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London closed higher on modest trade buying. Business was slow throughout the session, with the US raws market closed for the labour day holiday. October added $1.30 to close at $350.40, while December gained $2.00 to close at $346.00. There was no fresh news to give the market direction.

PAKISTAN - Sugar production in Pakistan in 1995/96 is officially estimated at 2.47 million tonnes, white value, down from 3.0 million tonnes produced the previous year. Internal demand is around 3 million tonnes so that the country is being forced to import significant amounts in 1995/96 to cover internal requirements.

An assessment of import needs is especially difficult as a lot of sugar is smuggled to nearby Iran and Afghanistan and the total in 1995/96 is put at 200,000 tonnes. While some believe production in 1996/97 could rise to 2.7 million tonnes, others believe that there will be no change at all and that production could even show a decline. In that case, the country will have to import more than the already contracted 500,000 tonnes.

DENMARK - Sugar exports in May 1996 amounted to 11,761 tonnes, raw value, down from 18,688 tonnes in May 1995. This brought cumulative exports in the first eight months of 1995/96 (October/May) up to 106,910 tonnes compared to 135,011 tonnes in 1994/95.

Total exports in 1994/95 reached 199,559 tonnes, down from 255,177 tonnes exported in 1993/94. Major countries of destination in October/May 1995/96 were Norway with 76,687 tonnes whites against 70,304 tonnes and Iceland with 5,779 tonnes against 5,621 tonnes.

NORWAY - Sugar imports in July 1996 amounted to 16,068 tonnes, raw value, up from last year's 15,590 tonnes. This brought cumulative imports in the first seven months of 1996 (January/July) up to 102,632 tonnes compared to 92,730 tonnes in the like period the previous year.

Total imports in 1995 amounted to 173,712 tonnes, down from 192,368 tonnes in 1994. Major countries of origin in January/July 1996 were Denmark with 61,174 tonnes whites compared to 61,580 tonnes and the United Kingdom with 23,779 tonnes against 19,833 tonnes.

CHINA - Sugar imports from Cuba started to pick up in July but Thailand's overall dominance of the market remained unchallenged in 1995/96. Sugar imports in July 1996 amounted to 196,402 tonnes, raw value, down from 213,913 tonnes in July 1995. This brought cumulative imports in the first eleven months of 1995/96 (September/July) up to 1.87 million tonnes, down from 2.68 million tonnes in 1994/95.

Total imports in 1994/95 amounted to 2.91 million tonnes against 1.33 million tonnes in 1993/94. Major countries of origin in September/July 1995/96 were Thailand with 628,067 tonnes raws against 907,465 tonnes, Cuba with 383,076 tonnes, down from 654,659 tonnes and Australia with 351,995 tonnes compared to 618,385 tonnes.

The largest supplier of white sugar was Thailand with 35,275 tonnes against 67,986 tonnes. Sugar exports in July 1996 reached 38,075 tonnes, up from 16,815 tonnes exported in July 1995. This brought cumulative exports in the first eleven months of 1995/96 (September/July) up to 784,194 tonnes compared to 509,998 tonnes in 1994/95.

Total exports in 1994/95 amounted to 540,004 tonnes against 1.10 million tonnes in 1993/94. Major countries of destination in September/July 1995/96 were Saudi Arabia with 263,445 tonnes whites against 102,164 tonnes, Indonesia with 153,888 tonnes compared to nil and Hong Kong with 83,908 tonnes against 36,455 tonnes.

GERMANY - The latest German beet test results show a satisfactory increase in root weight and sugar content which resulted in an above average rise of the sugar weight per ha. Beet weight per ha on 30 August 1996 amounted to 51.11 tonnes against 49.38 tonnes in 1995 and the five-year average (1991/95) of 49.71 tonnes.

Sugar content rose slightly to 15.3 per cent, down from 15.5 per cent in 1995 and also below the five-year average of 15.7 per cent. This resulted in a theoretical sugar weight per ha of 7.81 tonnes, white value, against 7.66 tonnes in 1995 and the average of 7.83 tonnes.

Given the high number of roots per ha in many regions and the high weight of leaves there is still good potential for improvement and average to slightly above average sugar yields seem to be within reach.
